FOR CLAT 2027
7

Blue Bond


• Sagarmala Finance Corporation Limited (SMFCL), India's state-
  owned maritime-focused lender, plans to launch the country's first
  blue bond during the financial year 2026-27.

• The bond will raise funds for maritime and coastal
  infrastructure projects while helping the corporation diversify its
  funding sources beyond traditional bank loans.

• This initiative marks India's entry into the global blue bond
  market, positioning the country alongside nations like Seychelles
  and Fiji in sustainable ocean finance.

Blue Bond

What is a Bond? –

• A bond is a debt instrument through which an entity
  (government or corporation) borrows money from investors for a
  specified period at a fixed or floating interest rate.

• The investor who buys the bond is essentially lending money to
  the issuer in return for periodic interest payments (called coupon)
  and the return of the principal amount on the maturity date.

• Bonds are traded in the secondary market, and their prices
  fluctuate inversely with changes in interest rates, making them a key
  fixed-income security.

Blue Bond


• A blue bond is a debt instrument designed specifically to raise
  capital for ocean-related and marine projects, including coastal
  ecosystem conservation and sustainable water management.

• Blue bonds function similarly to green bonds but focus exclusively on
  the blue economy.

• The concept aligns with UN Sustainable Development Goal 14
  (Life Below Water), which aims to conserve and sustainably use the
  oceans, seas and marine resources.

Blue Bond


• India has a coastline of over 7,500 kilometres and handles
  approximately 95% of its trade by volume through maritime
  routes, making ocean health critical to national prosperity.

• The country faces a significant maritime financing gap, with long-
  term infrastructure projects starved of affordable capital due to
  limited specialized financial institutions.

• Blue bonds offer a mechanism to attract ESG-focused domestic
  and global investors seeking sustainable investment opportunities
  with measurable environmental impact.

Blue Bond

Establishment of Sagarmala Finance Corporation –

• SMFCL was established in 2016 under the Ministry of Ports,
  Shipping and Waterways as Sagarmala Development Company
  Limited.

• It received a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) licence
  from the Reserve Bank of India on June 19, 2025, becoming India's
  first maritime-focused NBFC.

• The corporation has been granted Mini Ratna Category-I Central
  Public Sector Enterprise status, reflecting its strategic importance to
  the government.

Blue Bond


• SMFCL administers the government's ₹25,000 crore Maritime
  Development Fund (MDF), which includes a ₹20,000 crore Maritime
  Investment Fund and a ₹5,000 crore Interest Incentivisation Fund.

• The Interest Incentivisation Fund provides up to 3% interest
  subsidy to banks and financial institutions for loans given to Indian
  shipyards, addressing higher financing costs.

• The corporation plans to raise up to ₹1,000 crore through the blue
  bond issue, including a ₹500 crore greenshoe option.

Blue Bond


• NBFCs in India are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
  under Chapter III-B of the RBI Act, 1934, with registration
  requirements stipulated under Section 45-IA of the Act.

• The RBI Act requires NBFCs to maintain a Certificate of
  Registration (CoR) and satisfy minimum net owned fund
  requirements to carry on financial activities lawfully.

• SMFCL's registration as an NBFC subjects it to RBI's prudential norms,
  asset classification standards, and corporate governance
  requirements applicable to all non-banking financial companies.

Blue Bond

Blue Economy –

• The World Bank defines the blue economy as the sustainable use
  of ocean resources for economic growth, improved livelihoods and
  jobs while preserving ocean ecosystem health.

• It includes traditional sectors such as fisheries, ports and
  shipping, coastal tourism, and offshore oil and gas, alongside
  emerging areas like offshore wind and marine biotechnology.

• The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and
  Development (OECD) describes the sustainable blue economy as
  one that integrates economic, social and environmental dimensions
  for long-term ocean health.

Blue Bond


• India's blue economy contributes approximately 4% to the
  country's GDP and supports millions of livelihoods across coastal
  communities.

• Key sectors driving India's blue economy include fisheries (India is
  the world's third-largest fish producer), coastal tourism,
  renewable energy, and maritime trade.

• The Draft National Blue Economy Policy, placed in the public domain
  in February 2021 and revised in July 2022, covers seven
  thematic areas including ocean governance and marine spatial
  planning.

Blue Bond

Sagarmala Programme –

• Launched in March 2015, Sagarmala is the flagship initiative of the
  Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways aimed at promoting port-
  led development across India.

• As part of the programme, 845 projects worth approximately
  ₹6.06 lakh crore are under implementation, with 315 projects
  already completed at an investment of ₹1.57 lakh crore.

• The programme focuses on port modernization, port connectivity
  enhancement, port-led industrialization, and coastal community
  development.

Blue Bond


• Nine Indian ports are now among the world's top 100 ports,
  with Visakhapatnam (Vizag) ranked in the top 20 container ports
  globally.

• Maritime India Vision 2030 is a 10-year blueprint for the Indian
  maritime sector, superseding the Sagarmala programme and setting
  ambitious targets for port capacity and efficiency.

• By 2030, India aims to expand port capacity to 3,500 million
  tonnes per annum and make its ports fully digital and green.

Blue Bond


• Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 is a long-term roadmap for
  India's maritime resurgence, with investments of nearly ₹80 lakh
  crore earmarked for ports, coastal shipping, and inland waterways.

• Under this vision, India aims to achieve 4 million GRT of
  shipbuilding capacity and 10 billion metric tons of port
  handling annually, positioning India among the top five shipbuilding
  nations by 2047.

• The plan aims to generate 1.5 crore jobs and achieve net-zero
  emissions at all major ports by 2047, with green energy
  transition targets set for 2035.

Blue Bond

Framework for Blue Bonds –

• The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has introduced
  the concept of 'blue' and 'yellow' bonds as sub-categories of green
  debt securities within its regulatory framework.

• Blue bonds, as defined by SEBI, relate specifically to water
  management and the marine sector, providing a clear regulatory
  basis for such issuances in India.

• The framework requires issuers to appoint independent third-
  party reviewers to ensure alignment with recognized standards,
  mitigating the risk of misleading environmental claims.

Blue Bond


• SEBI unveiled a comprehensive ESG debt securities framework on
  June 5, 2025, covering social bonds, sustainability bonds, and
  sustainability-linked bonds under the NCS Regulations.

• The framework provides regulations for all stages—pre-issuance,
  post-issuance, and ongoing compliance related to reporting and
  verification of use of proceeds.

• These regulations aim to enhance transparency, standardise
  India's sustainable finance market, and prevent "purpose-washing" in
  ESG-labelled instruments.

Blue Bond


• Bond issuances in India are governed by the Companies Act, 2013,
  the SEBI (Issue and Listing of Non-Convertible Securities)
  Regulations, 2021, and the SEBI (Listing Obligations and
  Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015.

• The Ministry of Defence has amended guidelines to simplify the
  export authorization process for defence-related bonds, though blue
  bonds remain outside this specific purview.

• SMFCL's proposed blue bond will comply with all applicable SEBI
  regulations, including disclosure requirements, investor protection
  norms, and ongoing reporting obligations.

Blue Bond


• Seychelles issued the world's first sovereign blue bond in
  October 2018 with support from the World Bank, raising $15
  million to safeguard its ocean economy.

• The bond was structured with a $5 million partial credit guarantee
  to lower borrowing costs, reducing annual interest by approximately
  5%.

• The Bank of China issued Asia's first blue bond in 2020, raising
  funds for marine environmental protection and sustainable water
  resource management projects.

Blue Bond


• Blue bonds are issued by three types of entities: sovereign
  governments (Seychelles, Fiji), multilateral development banks and
  financial institutions (ADB, Nordic Investment Bank), and
  corporations.

• Sovereign issuers rely on fiscal guarantees, while development
  banks leverage strong credit ratings to attract private capital at
  scale.

• Corporations depend on market confidence and ESG credentials to
  issue blue bonds, often at premium pricing due to growing investor
  demand for sustainable instruments.

Blue Bond


• The global blue bond market is projected to reach $70 billion by
  2030, requiring simultaneous resolution of supply-side and demand-
  side constraints.

• Supply-side challenges include limited pipelines of investment-
  ready projects, institutional capacity gaps, and elevated perceptions
  of credit risk in ocean-related ventures.

• On the demand side, exclusion from major bond indices and weak
  benchmarking frameworks continue to limit investor participation in
  blue bonds.

Blue Bond


Recent News –

• The exact date for the blue bond issue has not been finalised,
  with the corporation awaiting conducive market conditions and
  stabilised yields.

• The blue bond is expected to be issued in the third quarter of the
  financial year 2026-27, subject to market stability.

Blue Bond


• Vadodara Municipal Corporation in Gujarat aims to raise up to
  ₹200 crore through a public blue bond issue for water-management
  projects.

• The funds will support sewage treatment plants, water supply
  augmentation, wastewater treatment facilities, and aquatic life
  protection projects.

• This would be India's first public blue municipal bond,
  potentially setting a precedent for other urban local bodies to access
  sustainable finance.

Ebola Outbreak


• On 17 May 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared
  the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)
  and Uganda a Public Health Emergency of International
  Concern (PHEIC).

• The declaration was made under the International Health
  Regulations (IHR) 2005.

• This is the WHO’s highest level of global health alert and calls
  for a coordinated international response to prevent further spread.

Ebola Outbreak

History –

• Ebola is a severe, often fatal zoonotic disease caused by viruses
  of the genus Orthoebolavirus, first identified in 1976 near the Ebola
  River in DRC.

• The virus spills over to humans from wild animals (fruit bats,
  non-human primates) and then spreads through direct contact
  with blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of
  infected persons.

• The disease has an average incubation period of 8–10 days
  (range 2–21 days) and symptoms include sudden fever, fatigue,
  muscle pain etc. and, in some cases, internal and external bleeding.

Ebola Outbreak


• Since 1976, there have been 36 documented outbreaks of Ebola,
  with the 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic being the
  largest (28,616 cases, 11,310 deaths).

• The current outbreak is DRC’s 17th Ebola outbreak since 1976 –
  the most of any country in the world.

• For the Bundibugyo strain, the case fatality rate in past outbreaks
  ranged from 30% to 50% , compared to up to 90% for the Zaire
  strain.

Ebola Outbreak

• Two Ebola vaccines have been licensed and prequalified by
  WHO:

 ➢The single-dose Ervebo (Merck)

 ➢The two-dose Zabdeno/Mvabea regimen (Janssen)

• However, these vaccines are not effective against the
  Bundibugyo strain, and no licensed vaccine or specific therapeutic
  currently exists for BVD.

• The WHO is relying on supportive care (rehydration, symptom
  management) , ring vaccination (using available vaccines as a
  preventive measure for contacts) techniques.

Ebola Outbreak


• Human-to-human transmission occurs through direct contact with
  blood, body fluids, or contaminated surfaces of an infected
  person or deceased individual.

• Healthcare workers are at high risk due to close contact with
  patients, especially when infection prevention and control (IPC)
  measures are inadequate.

• The WHO has reported at least four deaths among healthcare
  workers in the current outbreak.

Ebola Outbreak

Important Organizations –

• The WHO is a specialised agency of the United
  Nations established in 1948, responsible for international public
  health.

• Its primary role is to direct and coordinate global health
  responses, set norms and standards, and provide technical support
  to member states.

• The WHO has 194 member states and is governed by the World
  Health Assembly (WHA) and the Executive Board. Director
  General - Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.

Ebola Outbreak


• The International Health Regulations, 2005 (IHR) is a binding
  international legal instrument that entered into force on 15 June
  2007 and is binding on 196 countries, including all WHO member
  states.

• The IHR aim to prevent and control the international spread of
  disease while avoiding unnecessary interference with trade and
  travel.

• The PHEIC mechanism was established under the IHR. The first
  PHEIC was declared on 25 April 2009 for the H1N1 influenza
  pandemic.

Ebola Outbreak

• Since then, eight PHEICs have been declared:

 ➢2009–2010 H1N1 (Swine Flu) Pandemic, 2014 Polio
 Declaration (this PHEIC remains in effect for the international spread
 of wild poliovirus)

 ➢2013–2016 Ebola Outbreak (West Africa), 2015–2016 Zika Virus
 Epidemic, 2018–2020 Kivu Ebola Epidemic (DRC)

 ➢2020–2023 COVID-19 Pandemic

 ➢2022–2023 Mpox (Monkeypox) Outbreak

 ➢2024 Mpox Outbreak (Declared a new emergency due to a more
 lethal strain)

Ebola Outbreak


• The 77th World Health Assembly (June 2024) adopted a
  package of 300 amendments to the IHR, based on lessons from
  the COVID-19 pandemic.

• Key changes include the creation of a “pandemic emergency”
  alert (a higher level than PHEIC), a Coordinating Financial
  Mechanism, and a States Parties Committee for implementation.

• The amendments also introduce obligations to facilitate equitable
  access to medicines and vaccines and to promote a One Health
  approach.

Ebola Outbreak


• Under the IHR (2005), the WHO Director-General convenes
  an Emergency Committee of international experts to provide
  technical advice on whether an event constitutes a PHEIC.

• The committee is drawn from the IHR Experts Roster and includes
  experts in disease control, virology, vaccine development and
  infectious disease epidemiology.

• At least one member must be nominated by the State Party where
  the event arises, ensuring that the affected country’s views are
  heard.

Ebola Outbreak


• Under the IHR, each country must designate a National IHR Focal
  Point (NFP) responsible for communicating with WHO on public
  health events and emergencies.

• In India, the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), under
  the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, serves as the NFP.

• The NCDC also operates the Integrated Disease Surveillance
  Programme (IDSP) , which collects real-time data on disease
  outbreaks from across the country.

Ebola Outbreak


• The Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 is a colonial-era law that grants
  states temporary powers to take measures to prevent the spread of
  dangerous epidemic diseases.

• Section 2 of the Act allows state governments to prescribe special
  measures and regulate travel, inspection and detention of persons.

• The Act is silent on supply chain management, coordinated
  response mechanisms, surveillance, laboratories, and equity in access
  to countermeasures – exposing critical gaps in pandemic
  preparedness.

Ebola Outbreak


• The Disaster Management Act, 2005 treats health emergencies
  as merely one category of disaster, lacking the specialised provisions
  necessary for infectious disease control.

• It provides for the National Disaster Management Authority
  (NDMA) and State Disaster Management Authorities
  (SDMAs) , but coordination between central and state authorities
  has often proved difficult.

• Neither the Epidemic Diseases Act nor the Disaster Management Act
  was designed for the complexities of modern pandemic
  preparedness, leaving India’s legal framework fragmented.

Ebola Outbreak


• The government can activate the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 to
  screen passengers arriving from affected countries, isolate suspected
  cases, and issue quarantine orders.

• The Disaster Management Act, 2005 can be invoked to mobilise
  resources and coordinate a multi-sectoral response, including the
  deployment of rapid response teams.

• Legal experts have called for a dedicated Public Health
  Emergency Management Act (PHEMA) to clarify the division of
  powers and establish a unified command structure.

Ebola Outbreak


• India is a founding member of WHO and has been elected to
  the WHO Executive Board multiple times, most recently as chair
  of the 147th and 148th sessions.

• India has also been a strong advocate for reforming the IHR to
  ensure equity, solidarity and access to medical countermeasures for
  developing countries.

Ebola Outbreak

Recent News –

• The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus strain, one
  of three viruses known to cause large Ebola disease outbreaks
  (alongside Ebola virus and Sudan virus).

• As of May 2026, eight laboratory-confirmed cases, 246
  suspected cases and 80 suspected deaths have been reported
  in Ituri Province, DRC.

• Two imported cases (including one death) have been confirmed
  in Kampala, Uganda, with no apparent epidemiological link, indicating
  possible undetected community transmission.

Ebola Outbreak


• The WHO Director-General, after consulting the affected States
  Parties, determined that the event meets the legal definition of a
  PHEIC under Article 1 of the IHR (2005).

• Key factors:

  ➢ Extraordinary nature of the event (suspected cases in multiple
   provinces, high positivity rate, healthcare worker deaths);

  ➢ Risk of international spread (cases in Kampala and Kinshasa);
   and

  ➢ Significant uncertainties about the true number of infected
   persons.

Ebola Outbreak


• On 18 May 2026, Africa CDC declared the Ebola outbreak
  a PHECS under Article 3, Paragraph F of the Africa CDC Statute.

• The Africa CDC is a specialised technical institution of the African
  Union, established in 2017.

• Africa CDC and WHO are working jointly under the “4 Ones”
  principle – one team, one plan, one budget, one monitoring
  framework – to strengthen coordination and avoid duplication of
  efforts.

Ebola Outbreak


• As of 19 May 2026, the suspected toll had risen to 131 deaths and
  513 cases in DRC, with cases reported across Ituri and North Kivu
  provinces.

• The WHO is deeply concerned about the “scale and speed” of the
  outbreak, the high mobility of populations across borders, and
  the limited understanding of transmission patterns.

• The declaration does not constitute a pandemic
  emergency under the 2024 IHR amendments, because the spread
  remains largely regional.

Passage:

In 2026, the world witnessed renewed concern over an Ebola outbreak in Central
Africa, particularly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and parts of Uganda. The
outbreak involved the relatively rare ________ of the Ebola virus, for which no
approved vaccine currently exists. Health authorities and the Africa CDC, declared a
major international response due to the rapid spread of infections and the difficulty of
conducting surveillance in conflict-affected regions.

The outbreak highlighted challenges such as armed conflict, population displacement,
mistrust of health workers, and inadequate healthcare infrastructure. International
agencies launched emergency funding programmes and intensified cross-border
monitoring to prevent further transmission. WHO described the outbreak as one of the
largest Ebola emergencies in recent years.

Source: The Hindu

Ebola virus disease was first identified in 1976 in a region that is
now part of:

A. Sudan
B. Uganda
C. Democratic Republic of the Congo
D. Ethiopia
ANSWER - C

The declaration of a Public Health Emergency of International
Concern (PHEIC) is made by:

A. United Nations General Assembly
B. World Health Organization
C. Africa CDC
D. World Bank
ANSWER - B

The 2026 outbreak was primarily associated with which strain of Ebola?

A. Sudan strain
B. Zaire strain
C. Bundibugyo strain
D. Reston strain
ANSWER - C

Which of the following countries was the worst affected during the 2014–16
West African Ebola epidemic?

A. Sierra Leone, Liberia, and Guinea
B. Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda
C. Nigeria, Ghana, and Benin
D. Ethiopia, Sudan, and Chad
ANSWER - A

The headquarters of the World Health Organization is located in:

A. Vienna
B. Paris
C. Geneva
D. The Hague
ANSWER - C
